603.title: Whatever is born will pass
603.hook: jo upjio so binas hai: whatever is born will perish, today or tomorrow (Salok M9 52, ang 1429)
603.howItsDone: Sikhs hear salok fifty-two among Guru Tegh Bahadur's saloks at the close of every complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib.

segments.voice: Yesterday: chinta, and your line: nothing stays. Save worry for what can't happen; change is the road. Today, the next salok goes one step further.

A gardener plants tomatoes in May. By August the vines are taller than the fence and the kitchen counter is covered in fruit. By October the first frost comes, and in one night the whole bed goes black. The gardener knows this is coming. She plants anyway, every spring, and doesn't stand at the window in July grieving the frost. She picks, she cooks, she gives bags of tomatoes to the neighbors. The ending is written into the seed packet. Guru Tegh Bahadur's next salok says the same about everything that has ever been born, and then it says what to do with the summer.
screen: `TOMATOES IN MAY.` → `FROST IN OCTOBER.` → `THE ENDING IS IN THE SEED PACKET.`

segments.voice: Salok fifty-two, on Ang fourteen twenty-nine, begins: jo upjio so binas hai. Upjio is what has sprung up, been born, been made. Binas is what perishes, comes undone. Then three short words: paro aaj kai kaal. It falls today, or tomorrow. Kaal here means tomorrow, and some readers hear a shadow in it, since the same sound also names time, and death. The line doesn't say when, and it doesn't threaten. Only the date is open. The second line is where the salok turns. In paraphrase: Nanak says, sing the praises of the Lord, and let go of all the janjaal. Janjaal is a tangled word: the snares, the nets, the knots of busyness and attachment we get caught in, like a fishing net left in a shed for a year, knotted into itself. So the Guru puts two things side by side. Everything passes. Therefore, sing. Not therefore, despair; not therefore, nothing matters. The fact of passing is the reason to spend the time well. That's how the gardener lives. The frost isn't a reason not to plant. It's the reason to pick the tomatoes now and give some away. In Sikh life, singing the praises means the Name, kirtan, the daily banis. And Sikhs have a word for the frost's place in it: hukam, the order of things. Accepting that the frost comes is not the same as not caring about the garden.
screen: `UPJIO, BINAS: SPRUNG UP, COME UNDONE.` · `TODAY OR TOMORROW: ONLY THE DATE IS OPEN.` · `JANJAAL: THE TANGLED NET.` · `IT PASSES, SO SING.` · then, large: `TODAY OR TOMORROW.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you love that is passing: a season of your kids' lives, a friendship as it is right now, your own body at this age. Don't push the thought away or chase it into sadness; hold it the way you'd hold a ripe tomato, gently, because it won't keep, and think of one way to enjoy it today. If you pray, say Waheguru on the out-breath.
Janjaal, the snares and tangles of busyness. Whatever is born will pass, today or tomorrow, so sing, and let go of it while it's summer.
Your line: today or tomorrow. The frost is the reason to pick now. See you tomorrow.

604.title: Strength gone, in chains
604.hook: strength is gone, I'm in chains, nothing works; Nanak says, only You are my refuge (Salok M9 53, ang 1429)
604.howItsDone: Sikhs read salok fifty-three as part of the closing saloks of a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, and many turn to it in illness or trouble as a plain cry for the Lord's shelter.

segments.voice: Yesterday: janjaal, and your line: today or tomorrow. Everything passes, so sing. Today the saloks turn from the world to one person, at the end of their strength.

The calls have been made, the forms filled out, the advice taken, and the problem is still sitting there. A diagnosis. A job search in its ninth month. A child who won't talk to you. Everything known has been tried, and at some point a person hears themselves say, out loud or not: I've got nothing left. It's a strange, bare place. Pride doesn't work there; cleverness doesn't either. Guru Tegh Bahadur has a salok from exactly that place, and Sikh tradition hears it as the words of a man in a cell.
screen: `EVERYTHING TRIED.` → `I'VE GOT NOTHING LEFT.` → `A SALOK FROM THAT PLACE.`

segments.voice: Salok fifty-three, Ang fourteen twenty-nine. In paraphrase: my strength is exhausted, I am bound in chains, and nothing I try works. Nanak says, now You are my shelter, Lord: help me, as You helped the elephant. Three phrases do the work. Bal chhutkio: strength has slipped away. Bandhan pare: the bonds have fallen on me. Kachhoo na hot upaai: no remedy, no plan, nothing works. It's an honest inventory, with nothing dressed up. Then the turn: ab ot. Now, the shelter. Ot means a refuge, a support, the wall you put your back against. And the salok adds an old picture, gaj, the elephant. Indian tradition tells of an elephant king seized by a crocodile in a lake. He pulled for a long time with all his great strength and lost. Only when he gave up pulling and called on God was he freed. Gurbani recalls this story as a sign of grace for the helpless. Why does this salok weigh so much for Sikhs? Tradition places it in the Guru's last months, when he was imprisoned in Delhi before his execution, and Sikhs hear it as written in real chains. Historians don't know exactly when each salok was composed, so that link is tradition. Either way, the shape is the point. The salok doesn't pretend strength is limitless. It admits the end of strength, and from there it asks. In Sikh thought, that asking isn't failure. It's where the ot, the shelter, finally gets leaned on.
screen: `BAL CHHUTKIO: STRENGTH HAS SLIPPED AWAY.` · `NOTHING WORKS: AN HONEST LIST.` · `OT: THE SHELTER YOU LEAN ON.` · `THE ELEPHANT WHO STOPPED PULLING.` · then, large: `ONLY YOU.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one place where you've tried everything you know, and say it as plainly as the salok does: this is what I've tried; this is what isn't working. Then let yourself lean back, the way you'd lean against a wall. If you pray, ask God for help in your own words, or say Waheguru; if you don't, think of one person you could ask, and picture asking them.
Strength gone. Bal chhutkio, bandhan pare: strength slipped away, the bonds fell on me, and from there, the ot, the shelter.
Your line: only you. At the end of strength, asking isn't failure. Day six hundred four.

605.title: Strength returned
605.hook: strength has come, bonds are broken; tradition hears this as the young Gobind's answer (Salok 54, ang 1429)
605.howItsDone: Sikhs read saloks fifty-three and fifty-four together at the close of a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, and many tell the story of the father's letter and the son's reply when they do.

segments.voice: Yesterday: strength gone, and your line: only you. Today the very next salok answers it, almost word for word.

Picture a letter arriving from a prison. Inside, a father has written two lines: my strength is gone, I'm in chains, nothing works. Now picture the reply, written by his son, who is about nine years old. Sikh tradition tells exactly this story. It says Guru Tegh Bahadur, held in Delhi, sent yesterday's salok to Anandpur as a kind of question, and the young Gobind Rai, who would become Guru Gobind Singh, sent back an answer in the same meter, line for line. Whatever history finally says about how it happened, the two saloks sit next to each other in the Guru Granth Sahib, and they read like a call and a reply.
screen: `A LETTER FROM A PRISON.` → `A REPLY FROM A NINE-YEAR-OLD.` → `A CALL AND AN ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Put them side by side. Salok fifty-three said bal chhutkio: strength has slipped away. Salok fifty-four, on the same Ang, fourteen twenty-nine, says bal hoaa: strength has come. Fifty-three said bandhan pare: the bonds have fallen on me. Fifty-four says bandhan chhute: the bonds are broken. Fifty-three said nothing works; fifty-four, in paraphrase, says everything is possible. Then the second line: Nanak, all is in Your hands; You alone are the helper. Notice what didn't change. Both saloks end in the same place: God as the help. In fifty-three, the speaker leans on God because his own strength is gone. In fifty-four, the strength is back, and it's still God's. Its return doesn't become a reason for pride. We tend to pray when things are bad and forget when they're good. These two lines hold both seasons to the same shelter. The salok is printed among Guru Tegh Bahadur's saloks, and scholars differ on who composed it. Many Sikhs follow the tradition that it was the young Gobind's reply; others read it as the ninth Guru's own answer to his own question. The text doesn't settle it. What's certain is what came next in the story Sikhs tell: the father went to his death in Delhi in 1675, and the boy grew up to found the Khalsa. A child who could answer chains with strength returned. That's how the tradition remembers him.

606.title: All companions gone
606.hook: every companion left, none stayed to the end; only the Lord remains (Salok M9 55, ang 1429)
606.howItsDone: Salok fifty-five is read among the closing saloks of a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikhs remember Bhai Mati Das, Bhai Sati Das and Bhai Dayala, who stayed with Guru Tegh Bahadur in Delhi.

segments.voice: Yesterday: strength returned, and your line: all is in your hands. Today, a salok about who is still there when the hard part comes.
screen: `STRENGTH RETURNED — ALL IS IN YOUR HANDS.`

segments.voice: Hospital waiting rooms tell the truth about friendship. At the wedding there were two hundred people. At the birthday, the house was full. Then someone gets a long illness, and by the third month the visitors thin out. Nobody means it. People get busy; they don't know what to say; they assume someone else is going. And the patient notices, quietly, who is still coming on Tuesday afternoons. Guru Tegh Bahadur has a stark two-line salok about that thinning out. And the story around it holds a surprise.
screen: `TWO HUNDRED AT THE WEDDING.` → `THE VISITORS THIN OUT.` → `WHO STILL COMES ON TUESDAY.`

segments.voice: Salok fifty-five, Ang fourteen twenty-nine. In paraphrase: all my companions and friends have left me; no one kept company with me to the end. Nanak says, in this calamity, my one support is the Lord. Sang sakhaa: companions, friends. Sabh taj gae: all have gone. Kou na nibhio saath: no one saw the companionship through. Nibhaana is a rich Punjabi verb: to keep something going to the end, a promise, a friendship, faith when it costs. Then the second line: in this bipat, this disaster, the one tek, the one prop, is the Lord. The salok uses the name Raghunaath, a name for God that Gurbani borrows from the old stories of Rama. It continues the run we've been reading: Rama gone, nothing stays, strength gone. Now the people go too, and what remains is God. Here is the surprise. Sikh tradition remembers that when Guru Tegh Bahadur was held in Delhi, three Sikhs did stay with him: Bhai Mati Das, Bhai Sati Das, and Bhai Dayala. Tradition says they were executed in front of him, before his own death, and Sikhs remember them by name to this day. So the salok describes the way of the world, and the story honors the rare people who refused to be the way of the world. It names where the salok finds the final support. And it quietly asks: when someone you love is in the bipat, will you be the one who nibhaaes, who sees it through?

segments.voice: Remember a time someone stayed with you through something hard, who kept calling, who kept showing up, and thank them silently. Then think of someone in a long hard stretch now, an illness, a grief, a lonely year, and picture yourself as the Tuesday afternoon visitor, not the crowd at the wedding: a call, a meal dropped off, ten minutes sitting with them. If you pray, hold them before God and say Waheguru.
Tek, a prop, a support. Sang sakhaa sabh taj gae: everyone left, and in the bipat, the one tek is the Lord.
Your line: he remains. And now and then, so does a friend who sees it through. Day six hundred six.

607.title: The Name remains
607.hook: naam rahio saadhoo rahio: the Name remains, the holy remain, the Guru remains (Salok M9 56, ang 1429)
607.howItsDone: Salok fifty-six is read near the close of every complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikh teachers present it as the answer to the saloks about passing.

segments.voice: Yesterday: tek, and your line: he remains. When companions go, the one prop is the Lord. After a run of saloks about what goes, today's is about what stays.

For a week now these saloks have been taking things away. Rama and Ravana, gone. Youth, gone. Strength, gone. Friends, gone. Whatever is born will pass, today or tomorrow. Then comes salok fifty-six, and the whole list turns over. After all that subtraction, he finally names what doesn't go: three things, said in one breath, each with the same verb. And then a sting in the tail about how few people notice them.
screen: `A WEEK OF THINGS TAKEN AWAY.` → `THE LIST TURNS OVER.` → `THREE THINGS THAT DON'T GO.`

segments.voice: Salok fifty-six, Ang fourteen twenty-nine. Naam rahio, saadhoo rahio, rahio gur gobind. Rahio means remained, stayed, abides. The Name remains. The saadhoo, the holy one, the true devotee, remains. The Guru, God, remains. Three things, one verb, like three posts driven into ground that everything else is washing over. The Name, naam, stands at the center of Sikh devotion: God's presence, remembered and repeated. The saadhoo is the person who lives in that remembrance. Gurbani speaks often of the saadh sangat, the company of such people, and of how their example outlasts them. And gur gobind here isn't the tenth Guru's name: in this line it's God as Guru, the teacher who is also the Lord. The second line is the sting. In paraphrase: Nanak says, in this world, how rare is the one who has repeated the Guru's mantra. So the three things that last are there for anyone, and the salok says few pick them up. That's the shape of the whole collection. All week the world was a dream, a show, a wall of sand. That wasn't gloom for its own sake. It was clearing the table so you could see what was still on it. Everything on the table passes. The Name, the people who live it, and God are still there when the table is cleared.

segments.voice: Think back over what these saloks took away, youth, strength, friends who drifted, and then ask a different question: what has stayed? 608.title: Held in the heart
608.hook: I have held the Name in my heart; nothing equals it (Salok M9 57, ang 1429)
608.tomorrow: Saloks at the close of a reading
608.howItsDone: Salok fifty-seven is the last of Guru Tegh Bahadur's saloks and is read near the very end of every complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib.

segments.voice: Yesterday: rahio, and your line: still there when it's cleared. The Name, the holy and God remain. Today, salok fifty-seven, the last of Guru Tegh Bahadur's saloks.

Last words get remembered. An aunt's final sentence gets repeated at family gatherings for years. A letter's last line is the one people copy out and keep in a wallet. Guru Tegh Bahadur's saloks come near the very end of the Guru Granth Sahib, and the fifty-seventh, his last, sits close to the final page. After all the saloks about passing, about chains, about friends who leave, what does he choose to say last? Not a warning. Not a complaint. A plain statement of what he's holding on to.
screen: `LAST WORDS GET REMEMBERED.` → `THE FIFTY-SEVENTH SALOK.` → `WHAT HE CHOSE TO SAY LAST.`

segments.voice: Salok fifty-seven, Ang fourteen twenty-nine. Raam naam ur mai gahio: I have grasped the Name of the Lord in my heart. Ur is the heart, the chest, the place you'd press a hand to. Gahio is a grip word: seized, held tight, the way a climber holds a rope. Then: jaa kai sam nahee koi. Sam means equal. There is nothing equal to it. Raam here, as across Gurbani, is a name for the one God who pervades everything, not only the hero of the Ramayana. The second line, in paraphrase: remembering it, every trouble is erased, and the sight of You is granted. Sankat is a crisis, a tight spot. Daras is the sight of the beloved, the glimpse of God. Look at how the collection has moved. It started with the world as a dream and a wall of sand. It went through strength gone, chains, friends gone. Then the turn: the Name remains. And now the last word is personal: I have held it. Not the Name exists somewhere, but it is in my heart, gripped tight. Sikh tradition hears the whole set as the Guru's testimony near his martyrdom in Delhi, and this as its final line. Heard that way, this is a man about to lose everything the world can take, saying that the one thing he held couldn't be taken. Whatever the date of composition, that is how the tradition hears it.

609.title: Saloks at the close of a reading
609.hook: his saloks are read near the end of every complete reading of the Granth, often at a bhog for someone who has died
609.howItsDone: At the bhog of an akhand or sahaj path, the reader finishes the Guru Granth Sahib with Guru Tegh Bahadur's saloks and the Mundavani; Anand Sahib, Ardas, a hukamnama and karah prashad follow, and many families hold this after a death.

segments.voice: Yesterday: ur, and your line: nothing equals it. This week we read saloks fifty-two to fifty-seven: janjaal, strength gone, strength returned, tek, rahio, ur. Today: where Sikhs hear them.

A living room has been cleared of furniture. White sheets cover the floor. At one end, on a raised platform under a canopy, the Guru Granth Sahib lies open, and for several days, in shifts, family and friends have been reading it aloud from the first page to the last. A grandfather died ten days ago. Today is the last day of the reading. The house is full; someone is stirring a huge pot of karah prashad in the kitchen. And as the reader nears the last pages, the words that fill the room are the ones we've spent this month with.
screen: `WHITE SHEETS ON THE FLOOR.` → `A READING, FIRST PAGE TO LAST.` → `THE LAST DAY.`

segments.voice: A complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib is called a path. An akhand path runs without stopping, reader after reader, from the first page to the last. A sahaj path goes at an easier pace, over days or weeks. Either way, the reading ends with a ceremony called the bhog: the completion. Because the book has its order, every complete reading ends the same way. Near the very end come Guru Tegh Bahadur's saloks, then Guru Arjan's short Mundavani, the seal, and a last salok of his. Some sangats also read the Raagmala; Sikhs differ on that, and the Sikh code of conduct leaves it to local custom. Then the Anand Sahib is sung, the Ardas is said, a hukamnama, the day's word, is read, and karah prashad is shared. So Guru Tegh Bahadur's saloks are what the room hears just before a reading closes. Families often hold a sahaj path after a death, timed so the bhog falls on the day of the final prayers. The grieving family sits and hears: janjaal, today or tomorrow. All companions go. And then: rahio. The holy remain. I have held the Name in my heart; nothing equals it. The words were not written as funeral texts. They come at the end because of where they sit in the book. And in that room, they fit. They don't pretend the grandfather isn't gone. They name the passing out loud, and then they name what stays.
screen: `A PATH: THE WHOLE GRANTH, READ ALOUD.` · `THE BHOG: THE COMPLETION.` · `HIS SALOKS COME NEAR THE END.` · `THE ROOM HEARS PASSING, THEN WHAT STAYS.` · then, large: `READ FOR THE DEPARTED.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who has died, close or not so close, a grandparent, a friend, a teacher, and let their face come. Then slowly say three of the lines we've learned, pausing after each: janjaal, today or tomorrow; rahio; nothing equals it. You're not explaining anything, just keeping them company with the words, and if you pray, you can end with Waheguru.
Bhog, the completion ceremony. Guru Tegh Bahadur's saloks come just before it, so a grieving room hears both the passing and what stays.
